subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statement best describes sexual reproduction?
options: It involves the fusion of two gametes to form a genetically different offspring
It involves only one parent and produces identical offspring
It happens by mitosis without any gametes
It always produces offspring identical to one parent
questions.explain: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and the fusion of male and female gametes, giving offspring that vary genetically from their parents.

questions.q: Offspring produced by asexual reproduction are described as:
options: Genetically identical clones of the parent
Genetically different from the parent
A mixture of two parents' genes
Always haploid
questions.explain: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and mitosis, so the offspring are genetically identical clones.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of asexual reproduction over sexual reproduction?
options: Only one parent is needed, so reproduction can be rapid
It produces more genetic variation
It helps a population adapt to environmental change
It always requires two gametes to fuse
questions.explain: Asexual reproduction needs only one parent and no mate, allowing rapid population growth in stable conditions.

questions.q: Why does sexual reproduction produce variation in the offspring?
options: Gametes from two parents combine, mixing genetic information
The offspring are clones of one parent
No gametes are involved in the process
Mitosis copies the DNA exactly
questions.explain: Fusion of genetically different gametes from two parents mixes alleles, producing offspring that are genetically varied.

questions.q: Meiosis of one cell produces how many gametes, and of what type?
options: Four genetically different haploid cells
Two genetically identical diploid cells
Two haploid cells that are identical
Four diploid cells identical to the parent
questions.explain: Meiosis involves two divisions and produces four haploid gametes that are genetically different from one another.

questions.q: A human body cell contains 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a human gamete?
questions.explain: Gametes are haploid, containing one set of chromosomes (23 in humans), so fertilisation restores the diploid number of 46.

questions.q: How does meiosis differ from mitosis?
options: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces genetically varied cells
Meiosis keeps the chromosome number the same
Meiosis produces two identical diploid cells
Meiosis involves only a single cell division
questions.explain: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number from diploid to haploid and produces four genetically different cells, unlike mitosis.

questions.q: An organism has 8 chromosomes in each body cell. How many chromosomes will each of its gametes contain?
questions.explain: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so a gamete from an organism with 8 chromosomes contains 4.

questions.q: What is the structure of a DNA molecule?
options: A polymer of two strands coiled into a double helix
A single straight strand of protein
A branched chain of sugars
A single ring of amino acids
questions.explain: DNA is a polymer made of two strands forming a double helix, held together by complementary base pairs.

questions.q: In DNA, which bases pair together?
options: Adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine
Adenine with guanine, and cytosine with thymine
Adenine with cytosine, and thymine with guanine
Thymine with thymine, and guanine with guanine
questions.explain: Complementary base pairing means A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines a gene?
options: A section of DNA that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids to make a protein
The complete set of genetic material of an organism
A single base in a DNA molecule
A structure made only of protein found outside the nucleus
questions.explain: A gene is a short section of DNA that codes for a specific sequence of amino acids, and therefore a protein.

questions.q: What is meant by the genome of an organism?
options: The entire genetic material of that organism
A single chromosome
One gene on a chromosome
The proteins made by a cell
questions.explain: The genome is the entire genetic material (all the DNA) of an organism.

questions.q: One strand of DNA has the base sequence A-T-G-C. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
options: T-A-C-G
A-T-G-C
G-C-A-T
T-A-G-C
questions.explain: Using complementary base pairing (A-T, G-C), A-T-G-C pairs with T-A-C-G.

questions.q: What is an allele?
options: A different version of the same gene
A section of protein in a cell
A type of chromosome found only in gametes
The complete genome of an organism
questions.explain: Alleles are alternative versions of a gene that can give different characteristics.

questions.q: An individual with the genotype BB is best described as:
options: Homozygous dominant
Heterozygous
Homozygous recessive
Haploid
questions.explain: Two identical dominant alleles (BB) means the individual is homozygous dominant.

questions.q: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
options: Genotype is the alleles present; phenotype is the physical characteristics shown
Genotype is the physical appearance; phenotype is the alleles present
They both describe only the environment
Genotype refers only to recessive alleles
questions.explain: Genotype is the combination of alleles an organism has, while phenotype is the observable characteristics it produces.

questions.q: Two heterozygous plants (Tt) are crossed. What is the expected ratio of tall (T dominant) to short (t recessive) offspring?
options: 3 tall : 1 short
1 tall : 1 short
2 tall : 2 short
4 tall : 0 short
questions.explain: A Tt x Tt cross gives genotypes TT, Tt, Tt, tt, producing a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.

questions.q: A cross is carried out between a heterozygous individual (Bb) and a homozygous recessive individual (bb). What is the expected phenotype ratio?
options: 1 dominant : 1 recessive
3 dominant : 1 recessive
All dominant
All recessive
questions.explain: Bb x bb produces Bb and bb offspring in equal numbers, giving a 1:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.

questions.q: How can mutations lead to variation within a population?
options: They change the DNA base sequence and can create new alleles
They always remove genes from the genome
They make all offspring genetically identical
They only occur during asexual reproduction
questions.explain: A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence that can produce a new allele, contributing to genetic variation.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of continuous variation?
options: Human height
Blood group
Whether earlobes are attached or free
Ability to roll the tongue
questions.explain: Continuous variation shows a range of values with no distinct categories, such as human height.
